2026 Midterm Election Results

Governors, Senate, and House results from Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, 2026, drawn as cartograms: states sized by 2020 Census population, House districts as equal tiles — and, under each, the same results on a contiguous diffusion cartogram, where the shapes keep their borders and area carries the population. Colour is the winning party — blue for Democrats, red for Republicans — shaded by the winner’s vote share in five bins, pale under 55% and deepest at 85% or more.

Results as of Sunday, November 8, 2026, ~4:30 p.m. PT — five days after Election Day. Results are unofficial; states certify in the coming weeks, and a “call” is a news organisation’s projection, not an official result. 14 races are still uncalled, and two Louisiana House seats go to runoffs on December 12.

Sources: Wikipedia’s 2026 gubernatorial, Senate, and House election pages (revisions of Nov 8), cross-checked against AP call status, Ballotpedia, and Poliwave. House vote shares are AP data last updated Nov 5–6.

View 01 · Governors

Governors — 36 races

Each square is a state, sized by its 2020 Census population (a Demers cartogram). Democrats flipped five governorships — Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio, and Texas — and hold a majority of governorships for the first time since 2009: 28–20 overall, with Alaska and Kansas still to come.

Democrats 22 · Republicans 12 · 2 uncalled (AK, KS) · 14 states had no race

Contiguous diffusion · Governors

The same 36 races, with the states keeping their shapes and borders: area is stretched until it matches each state’s share of the 2020 Census population. Hovering here highlights the same state in the squares above.

Loading the contiguous cartogram…

The 14 grey states — DE, IN, KY, LA, MS, MO, MT, NJ, NC, ND, UT, VA, WA, WV — elect their governors in other years. Alaska is ranked-choice: the shares shown are first-choice votes, not a final margin. Kansas, at 0.6 points with ~99% counted, is the closest governor’s race in the country.

Contiguous geometry: precomputed go-cart diffusion cartogram (Gastner–Seguy–More, go-cart-wasm 0.5.0), area ∝ 2020 Census population — mean area error 0.021%, worst Alaska +0.95%, 107/107 adjacencies preserved. Alaska and Hawaii are drawn as insets, not at their true positions, so the view uses an identity projection rather than Albers USA.

View 02 · Senate

Senate — 35 seats up

Same cartogram, coloured only where a seat was contested: 33 Class 2 seats plus Class 3 special elections in Florida and Ohio. Democrats flipped eight seats — Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Mississippi, North Carolina, Ohio (special), South Carolina, and Texas — and lost none of their own. The chamber stands 55–44 on called races, with Alaska pending.

View 03 · House

House — 435 districts

Every voting district is one equal tile, laid out to keep neighbours neighbours (the squared-cost tile grid). Democrats won control of the House; only two seats flipped Republican all night — TN-09 and TX-32. If all 11 current leaders held, the House would finish 261–174.

Democrats 256 · Republicans 168 · 11 uncalled · popular vote D 55.7% / R 42.8%

Contiguous diffusion · House

The same 435 districts with their real shapes kept, area stretched to 2020 Census population. District populations are near-equal by design, so this map stays close to the undistorted shapes — what changes is the colour, not the size. Hovering here highlights the same district in the tiles above.

Loading the contiguous cartogram…

435 voting districts only — the six non-voting delegates (DC, Puerto Rico, and the territories) are excluded. California accounts for two of the uncalled races, mostly mail-ballot backlog rather than close counts; MN-01, NC-03, and NC-05 are effectively tied.

Contiguous geometry: precomputed go-cart diffusion cartogram (Gastner–Seguy–More, go-cart-wasm 0.5.0), area ∝ 2020 Census population — delivered mean area error 0.084% (raw solver 0.018%); AZ-02’s +6.33% is a repair artefact from fixing self-intersecting geometry, not solver error; 1,134/1,134 adjacencies preserved. Alaska and Hawaii are drawn as insets, not at their true positions, so the view uses an identity projection rather than Albers USA.

Reading the fine print

What is still shaky

  • House vote shares lag the calls. The percentages come from AP data last updated Nov 5–6, while the calls are as of Nov 13 — so a share may have moved by about a point since. The winners will not have.
  • Two called races the AP had not called (as of its Nov 6 data): TN-04 (Broderick, D, +0.2) and ME-02 (LePage, R, +1.6). Of the two, only TN-04 is a genuine recount risk.
  • FL-10 has no published vote totals — the AP called it for Maxwell Frost (D) at poll close with 0% counted, so it is shaded at mid-depth with no margin.
  • Alaska is ranked-choice everywhere — governor, Senate, and its single House seat. First-choice shares are not final margins, and the Senate race has no published shares at all yet.
  • Louisiana decides two seats on December 12: LA-05 (Moore, D, vs Firment, R) and LA-06 (Banks, D, vs Miguez, R) go to runoffs after a jungle primary. Their tiles are marked as runoffs, not party wins.
  • Callers disagree by an hour and a seat or two. These tallies follow AP race calls as of Nov 13; at the same moment Decision Desk HQ had called two more House races — CA-04 and CA-23 — which the AP still has as Too Early to Call. That is caller lag, not an error in either.

Six more House calls since Tue Nov 10: AZ-02 for Eli Crane (R), 163,530 to 160,084 (49.6%–48.6%), AP Mon Nov 9; CA-07 for Doris Matsui (D), 131,864 to 119,664 (52.4%–47.6%), AP Tue Nov 10; CA-40 for Ken Calvert (R), 121,327 to 108,322 (52.8%–47.2%), AP Mon Nov 9; CO-04 for Eileen Laubacher (D), 187,745 to 184,220 (48.8%–47.9%), a Democratic flip — Boebert has not conceded; FL-07 for Ryan Elijah (R), 161,300 to 159,669 (49.7%–49.2%), no recount at 0.503 points, just outside the 0.5-pt threshold; WA-05 for Michael Baumgartner (R), 163,593 to 149,654 (52.2%–47.8%), AP Nov 9. House tally now D 256 / R 168, 11 uncalled. California’s two remaining uncalled races, CA-04 and CA-23, the AP still has as Too Early to Call — Decision Desk HQ has called both, the AP has not. Mississippi Senate called: the AP called it for Scott Colom (D) Wed Nov 11, 5:58 p.m. ET, 473,336 to 468,667 (49.2%–48.7%), a 4,669-vote margin; Hyde-Smith conceded that evening. Alaska: Peltola leads Sullivan by 5,800 (125,157 to 119,357, 49.2%–47.0%), ~88% counted; another batch lands today, ranked-choice tabulation Wed Nov 18, certification targeted Nov 25. Florida certifies Tue Nov 17; LA-05 and LA-06 runoffs Sat Dec 12.

Methods note

Methods: why this colour scale

The chart below plots the perceptual lightness (CIELAB L*) of every colour in Wikipedia’s Presidential palettes (WP:USALEGEND) against the OKLCH-calibrated Fix 1 ramps, across all eight vote-share brackets. L* is recomputed from the hex values (sRGB, D65 white point), not taken from any published table. Wikipedia’s failures reproduce exactly: the Republican line nearly stops between 60–70% and 70–80% (ΔL* −1.9, landing on exactly the Democratic L* of 44.2 — a cross-party gap of 0.0), the light Democratic end is compressed (20–30% → 30–40% steps only −3.0), and at 90–100% the two parties sit just 3.9 L* apart. The Fix 1 curves fix the shape instead: even steps of −7.0 to −10.8 per bracket, and nothing below L* 27.5 (the dashed line).

Loading the L* trajectory chart…

Each dot is filled with the actual shade at that bracket, so the points themselves darken as the lines descend — pale at the light end, near-black at the dark end.

Correction. The Fix 1 table this chart was drawn from claims a dark-tail cross-party gap of 5.8 at 90–100%. Recomputed from the hexes, the gap is 3.0 — Republican #911108 at L* 30.5 against Democratic #043A97 at L* 27.5. The extremes stay distinguishable by hue and chroma — deep vermilion against deep cobalt — not by lightness alone.

Scope. The maps on this page use the Fix 2 five-bin scale, keyed to the winner’s vote share — not the scale drawn here. The chart shows Fix 1 (eight brackets) because it preserves Wikipedia’s bracket structure, so the curves are directly comparable; do not read the charted colours as the ones on the maps above.

Not charted. The Proposal palette does not appear: only its 90–100% extremes were supplied, so drawing it a curve would be invented data.

Geometry: state squares from the Demers layout (side ∝ √2020 Census population) and the squared-cost district tile grid built for this site’s cartogram pages; contiguous views are the precomputed go-cart-wasm 0.5.0 diffusion cartograms (states and 435 districts), shipped as TopoJSON and drawn with an identity projection (Y reflected) because Alaska and Hawaii are insets in those files. Full data, sources, and methodology: the three Wikipedia 2026 election pages — governors, Senate, House — with AP results, Ballotpedia, and Daily Letter’s AP race pages as cross-checks.
